aliases.name: นางไม้
aliases.meaning: Lady of the Tree / Wood Lady

description.summary: A general Thai folkloric category of female spirits that inhabit large trees. Specific named tree spirits — including Nang Tani and Nang Ta-khian — are types of Nang Mai. The male equivalent is the Rukkhadeva.
description.full: Nang Mai (Thai: นางไม้, 'Lady of the Tree') is the generic Thai folkloric category for female ghosts or spirits that inhabit large trees. Specific named tree spirits — most prominently Nang Tani (of the wild Musa acuminata banana tree) and Nang Ta-khian (of the takhian, Hopea odorata) — are understood as particular instances of Nang Mai. Nang Mai are typically described as young women in pleated traditional Thai dress with shoulder-length hair, said to inhabit invisible 'palaces' within the canopies of their trees. The male equivalent is the Rukkhadeva (รุกขเทวดา), a Pali-derived term for a tree deity who tends to inhabit larger trees such as the banyan. Beliefs around Nang Mai are pragmatic as well as devotional: they are invoked to deter the felling of large trees, with folklore warning that a tree-cutter who disturbs a Nang Mai's home will be cursed, sicken, or lose their mind. Modern offerings include traditional Thai costumes, perfumes, and cosmetic kits, and Thai villagers commonly mark spirit trees with multicoloured (often three-coloured) cloth bands. The tradition is integrated with Theravada Buddhist practice in Thailand: monastic precepts forbidding the cutting of fresh vegetation are widely understood to honor tree spirits, and folk practice happily compromises between formal Buddhism and local animist veneration.

etymology.origin: Thai นาง (nang, 'lady') + ไม้ (mai, 'wood, tree').
etymology.meaning: Literally 'Lady of the Tree' or 'Wood Lady'.
etymology.first_use: Long-standing Thai folk-religious usage; precise textual emergence undated.

features.description: Manifests as a beautiful young woman in traditional Thai pleated dress and sash, with shoulder-length hair
Tied to a specific tree, in which she inhabits an invisible 'palace'

physical.morphology: A culturally specific class of human-form female tree spirits.

abilities.description: Believed to curse, sicken, or madden anyone who fells the tree she inhabits; potency correlates with the size and sap of the tree
Benevolent Nang Mai may warn their owners of upcoming danger
Some Nang Mai are said to lure men, taking them as husbands or, in malevolent variants, killing them

patterns: Intervenes when the tree is threatened
Receives offerings of cloth, costumes, cosmetics, and food at the base of the tree

range.description: Nang Mai veneration is found throughout Thailand and in adjacent Theravada-Buddhist Southeast Asia.

hotspots.name: Sao Ronghai (Chao Mae Takhian Tong Shrine)
hotspots.notes: Notable shrine featuring a legendary golden teak pillar believed to house a Nang Mai, with origin mythology connected to Bangkok's founding

origins.cultural_roots: Indigenous Thai animism integrated with Theravada Buddhist practice; cognate with broader Southeast Asian tree-spirit traditions.
origins.earliest_accounts: Long-standing oral tradition; recorded in modern Thai folkloric and ethnographic writing.
origins.folklore_connections: Cognate with other Southeast Asian tree-spirit traditions and with Buddhist Rukkhadeva traditions.

history.modern_era: Nang Mai veneration remains widely practiced in Thailand. Large trees are routinely marked with multicoloured cloth bands and small shrines, especially at temple grounds, village edges, and along rural roads, and the Sao Ronghai (Chao Mae Takhian Tong Shrine) in Saraburi is a notable contemporary site.

paranormal.name: Animist tree spirits
paranormal.description: Traditional Thai animist understanding of Nang Mai as real spiritual beings inhabiting and protecting individual large trees.
evidence_cited: Ubiquitous marking of large trees with coloured cloth

skeptical.name: Cultural-ecological function
skeptical.description: Anthropological reading: Nang Mai beliefs function as a cultural mechanism for the conservation of large trees, by attaching strong taboos to felling them.
proponents: Folklorists and anthropologists of Thai religion
evidence_cited: Practical preservation of large trees near villages

traditions: Tying of multicoloured cloth bands around spirit trees
Offerings of Thai costumes, perfumes, and cosmetics at the base of spirit trees
stories: Marriage ceremonies between young men and tree spirits, with offerings of pig head, alcohol, duck, chicken, and fruit performed on Tuesdays or Saturdays
folklore.beliefs: Nang Mai are integrated with Theravada Buddhism: monastic precepts forbidding the cutting of fresh vegetation are popularly understood to respect tree spirits.

research.ongoing_studies: Studied within Thai folklore studies and Southeast Asian religion.
